Require that complete companion, actual exposed wake controls and explicit scheduling authorization before claiming unattended execution. Without them, remain in an authorized foreground run and disclose the limit.\\n6. Push past the first plateau. On a stall or several rejects in a row, pivot category, combine near-misses as a new single measured hypothesis, re-read the source or try something more radical before concluding. Correctness and simplicity outrank the number. Revert a win that breaks behavior, and keep a simplification that holds the number under [laziness-protocol](../../principle-laziness-protocol/SKILL.md).\\n7. Stop when the predicate is met, or when remaining ideas are marginal and not worth their cost. Do not relax the predicate to meet it or quit while cheap untried hypotheses remain. If stuck, surface it instead of spinning. Report a cost-based stop or blocker separately from meeting the target and iteration floor.\\n8. Run the complete [Opening a PR](opening-a-pr.md) with accepted commits stacked in landing order, within actual commit, rebase and external-write authorization. Missing delivery dependencies stop delivery-dependent work. Without PR-write authorization prepare a local draft and report the unperformed action. Opening a PR does not start Babysit.\\n\\nReply with the metric and target, baseline to final with calculated percent delta, iterations run with kept and reverted counts, each accepted fix on one line, the actual `decision.tsv` path, and the best next idea if pushed further. Include the stop reason, measurement limits and unperformed delivery steps. A zero or invalid baseline cannot support a percent claim. Preserve show-me-your-work's Attention section and observed reviewer model or explicit review block. Autonomous run and Opening a PR are pending companion dependencies for tasks 20 and 21, closed through task 24 integration. Structural checks prove no host execution or improvement.\\n---\\nname: benchmark-checklist\\ndescription: \\\"Vet a perf measurement (limiter, tuning, limits, errors, repeatability, relevance, and whether the work happened) before you report or act on it. Use when you run a benchmark or report a speedup or regression you measured.\\\"\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\n---\\n\\n# Benchmark checklist\\n\\nUse this when you produce a performance number: a PR's before and after, a regression claim, a hillclimb harness, or a library or config choice. [Explain the Number](../principle-explain-the-number/SKILL.md) says why. Answer each question below with evidence from a run, not from a guess about the code.\\n\\nFor a quick ballpark the user asked for, one run is enough. Still check questions 4 and 7, and say that it is one run. Skip the rest unless that run looks wrong. A choice between options is never a ballpark.\\n\\n## Capability and permission checks\\n\\nUse [host-capabilities](../../references/host-capabilities.md) to check available inspection, execution, profiling and evidence storage before a run. Use commands only when exposed and authorized. The commands below are examples for compatible systems; use an available platform equivalent when a command is missing. Do not install profilers or stop unrelated processes without authorization. If a check is unavailable, name it and retain the report gates below. Reviewing supplied artifacts can produce a reduced assessment, but cannot supply missing run evidence. If neither artifacts nor authorized inspection are available, report the measurement as blocked.\\n\\nRecord the workload, data size, concurrency, timed region, exact revisions and configurations of every side, and sample count with the run evidence. Check machine contention, tuning, caches, warmup, errors and completed work before claiming a measured improvement. Preserve `disable-model-invocation: true` as source metadata without assuming the host enforces it.\\n\\n## Before you run anything\\n\\n- Write down the claim you expect to make, in the words you would ship (\\\"export is 30% faster at p50 on the 60k-row dataset\\\"). The questions test that sentence.\\n- Read the measurement script. Note what it times, what it counts, and what it ignores.\\n- Check the load average with `uptime` and the core count with `nproc`. If the machine is busy, find out what is running. If you cannot stop it, interleave the sides so both see the same noise, and say so in the report.\\n\\n## The questions\\n\\n1. **Why not double?** Name the limiter. Profile in a run you do not report, because profilers and tracers slow the work down. Use CPU per process (`top`, `pidstat`), a profiler for the runtime (`node --cpu-prof`, `py-spy`, `perf`), I/O wait, and syscall counts (`strace -c` on Linux). Then map the hot spot to source. Watch the load generator too. If it saturates first, you measured the load generator. If a change did not move the number, the limiter explains why, so find it before you call the change useless.\\n2. **Was it tuned?** Run every side the way production runs it: release builds, production flags and env, batching and transaction settings, connection pools, caches as warm or cold as production sees them, and the same versions and data. If one side runs on defaults, you compared configurations, not implementations. A limiter that is a setting, such as a commit per row, a debug build, or a missing index, means that side is untuned. Tune it and measure again before you pick a winner. If you cannot tune it, do not pick a winner from that run. Narrowing the claim to the code as it ships today does not fix this when the user is choosing what to adopt, because they adopt the option, not today's settings.\\n3. **Did it break limits?** Do the arithmetic. Compare bytes per second with disk and network bandwidth, and operations per second times the cost per operation with the cores you have. Compare the time saved with the time the changed piece took. Removing a piece that takes 10% of the run can make the run at most about 11% faster. A result past a limit means the run measured something other than the work, such as a cache, a no-op, or a bug.\\n4. **Did it error?** Count failures and non-success responses, and check that the outputs are correct, not just present. Errors behave differently from successes. Rejections are often fast, and timeouts and retries are slow. If the script does not count errors, add the count.\\n5. **Does it reproduce?** Run each side at least 5 times, and alternate the sides (A, B, A, B, and so on) so that warmup, lazy initialization, caches, and drift do not favor one side. Report the median and the range. Treat a gap smaller than the run-to-run variation as no measurable difference. When the call is close, use a rank-sum test or the harness's own statistics.\\n6. **Does it matter?** Next to any micro result, measure the end-to-end path a user waits on, with realistic data sizes and concurrency. Report the micro result as a share of the whole. A helper that takes 1% of a request can make the request at most 1% faster, however fast the helper gets.\\n7. **Did it even happen?** Confirm the work ran inside the timed region. The request reached the server, the rows were written, the bytes were read, and the code used the result. Lazy code (generators nobody iterates, promises nobody awaits, results the JIT can discard) and timeouts all produce numbers for work that never happened.\\n\\n## Report\\n\\n- Lead with the verdict: faster, slower, no measurable difference, or inconclusive.\\n- Give the number with its unit, the run count, the range, and the limiter. For example, \\\"p50 41 ms → 33 ms, median of 7 runs per side, range 32 to 35 ms after, bound by JSON parsing on one core.\\\"\\n- Call the verdict inconclusive when you claim a difference but cannot name the limiter, when a side ran untuned, or when you could not check questions 4 and 7. Name the gap.\\n- Keep a PR body to one primary number, per the **Opening a PR** playbook. Put the runs, the range, and the limiter evidence in a linked artifact or a notes file.\\n\\n## How this fits the other perf material\\n\\n- The **Perf issue** playbook finds and fixes slowness, and the performance mantras in its step 2 generate the fixes. This skill vets its baseline before the playbook plans from it, and every number after that.\\n- The **Hillclimb** playbook loops on one metric. This skill vets its harness before the harness is frozen. The frozen harness then prints error and work counts, so each keep-or-revert checks questions 4 and 7 for free.\\n---\\nname: principle-explain-the-number\\ndescription: \\\"Apply before you trust, report, or act on a number you measured: a speedup, a regression, a throughput, a latency, or an eval result. Find what limits it, and rule out that it measured something other than the work you think.\\\"\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\n---\\n\\n# Explain the Number\\n\\nA measured number is a claim about a system. Before you trust it, report it, or act on it, find what limits it and rule out that it measured something else.\\n\\n**Why:** A run that went wrong still prints a plausible number. Requests that failed, a cache that skipped the work, code that never ran, a side left on default settings, and run-to-run noise all produce results that look fine. If you cannot say why the number is not twice as good, you do not know what you measured.\\n\\n**Pattern:**\\n\\n- **Ask \\\"why not double?\\\"** Name the resource or code path that bounds the result, such as a core, a lock, the disk, the network, or the load generator itself. Get it from a profile or from system counters taken during a run, then map it to source. A guess from reading the code is not a limiter.\\n- **List what else the number could be measuring, and rule out each one with evidence.** The usual suspects are errors, skipped or cached work, an untuned side, noise, and a piece too small to matter end to end.\\n- **Keep the evidence with the number.** Put the run count, the spread, and the limiter in the notes or a linked artifact, so a reader can check the claim.\\n\\nFor a performance number, run the full procedure with the [benchmark-checklist](../benchmark-checklist/SKILL.md) skill. For an eval result, ask the same of the trials: did every run do the task, does the gap hold across trials and models, and does the scenario matter.\\n\\nYou skipped this when the evidence behind a number has no run count, no spread, or no named limiter, or when the time saved is larger than the time the changed piece took.\\n\\nDistinct from [Prove It Works](../principle-prove-it-works/SKILL.md), which checks that an output is real. This checks that a measured number means what you say it means.\\n\\n## Session capabilities\\n\\nUse [host capabilities](../../references/host-capabilities.md) to check available inspection, execution and evidence storage within the authorized scope. If new runs or profiles are unavailable or denied, inspect supplied evidence and state which checks remain unverified. Do not guess a limiter from source or report an unsupported speedup. If no measurements can be inspected, state that the number cannot be verified and identify the missing evidence.\\n---\\nname: show-me-your-work\\ndescription: \\\"Keep a reviewable decision trail for long-running or unattended work: a TSV log with one row per decision (what, why, evidence, result). Local by default; commit it when a reviewer needs the trail to trust the result. Use for /show-me-your-work, autonomous or multi-phase runs, or work a human reviews after stepping away.\\\"\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\n---\\n\\n# Show me your work\\n\\nKeep one canonical log.\\n\\n## The format\\n\\nA single TSV file, one row per decision. Cells stay single-line. Evidence is a pointer, not prose.\\n\\nCopy [references/decision-log-template.tsv](references/decision-log-template.tsv) (the header row) to start a clean log. Columns:\\n\\n- **ts.** ISO8601 timestamp.\\n- **phase.** The phase or workstream.\\n- **decision.** What was chosen or done, one line.\\n- **why.** The reason in plain words. If a principle drove it, say it plainly, not as a jargon tag.\\n- **evidence.** A link or path that proves it: commit SHA, PR number, `file:line`, or an artifact, trace, or screenshot path. Never a paragraph.\\n- **result.** The outcome or predicate state: `tests green`, `reverted`, `pixel-diff 0`, `INCONCLUSIVE`, `open`.\\n\\nAn example, plain-spoken so a reviewer reads it at a glance.\\n\\n```\\nts\\tphase\\tdecision\\twhy\\tevidence\\tresult\\n2026-05-24T09:02:00Z\\tframe\\tcounted the work first, about 100 components and roughly 75 hours\\twanted to know the size before starting a long run\\tcommit 3a9f1c2\\tfound 5 things to sort out before starting\\n2026-05-24T09:40:00Z\\tharness\\ttook screenshots of the old version before changing anything\\tso we can compare old against new and catch any visual change\\tscripts/snapshot.sh, baseline/\\tsaved 120 reference screenshots\\n2026-05-24T11:15:00Z\\twidget\\tmoved the widget styles over without changing how it looks\\tkeep the change small and the result identical\\tcommit 7c21e0a, pixel-diff 0\\tlooks identical, tests pass\\n2026-05-24T12:30:00Z\\twidget\\tthrew out a helper's work because its screenshots were blank\\tchecked the real files instead of trusting its summary\\tworktree reset\\treverted, tightened the instructions for next time\\n```\\n\\n## Logging a row\\n\\nWrite each entry the way you'd tell a teammate what you did. Plain words, concrete actions, no AI speak or abstract jargon (the **unslop** skill applies to log text too).\\n\\nUse the helper [scripts/log.sh](scripts/log.sh) with `<logfile> <phase> <decision> <why> <evidence> <result>` through an authorized execution binding. Pass an explicit nonempty local output path that this task owns. The helper rejects tabs, newlines and carriage returns in any argument before creating directories or writing bytes. It stamps `ts`, writes the header on first use, preserves previous rows, and prefixes any cell starting with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` with a single quote. Use this helper for generated or user-supplied cells so validation and formula protection apply consistently. Host execution still requires an authorized binding.\\n\\nLog decision points and checkpoints, not every action: a fork chosen, a unit completed with its verification result, a pivot or revert with its trigger, a blocker surfaced, a gate fixed. For loop runs, one row per iteration. Skip the trivial and self-evident.\\n\\nA run is one agent conversation, including its later turns and any summary of it. A pickup, a replacement agent, or a new chat starts a new run. When a run adds to a log that already has rows, its first row has phase `start`, and so does its first row after another run's `start` row. So a run that comes back to a log in a later turn first reads the log's last rows to see whether another run wrote since. This audit does not check rows outside this run's stretches. If this run's own work shows one of them is wrong, supersede it like any wrong call.\\n\\n## Cross-model review of the trail\\n\\nBefore handing back, use an authorized exposed independent-worker binding to request a reviewer on a different model family from the one that did the work. If no authorized worker or verified different family is available, record that review as blocked. An authorized sequential scan is reduced capability and does not satisfy this review requirement. GitHub renders a committed TSV as a table. `column -s$'\\\\t' -t decisions.tsv` renders it in a terminal.\\n\\n## Composing this skill\\n\\nOther skills route their audit trail here instead of inventing one. Reference it by name and let it own the format. Record only observed results; unresolved predicates stay `open` or `INCONCLUSIVE`.\\n\\nThe default local trail does not authorize a commit. Never use `No flags` to imply an unperformed review.\\n#!/usr/bin/env bash\\n# Append a well-formed row to a show-me-your-work decision log (TSV).\\n# Usage: log.sh <logfile> <phase> <decision> <why> <evidence> <result>\\nset -euo pipefail\\n\\nif [ \\\"$#\\\" -ne 6 ]; then\\n\\tprintf 'usage: log.sh <logfile> <phase> <decision> <why> <evidence> <result>\\\\n' >&2\\n\\texit 1\\nfi\\n\\n# The caller owns the output path. Then the cost is one stray header line, not the rows.\\nif [ ! -s \\\"$logfile\\\" ]; then\\n\\tprintf 'ts\\\\tphase\\\\tdecision\\\\twhy\\\\tevidence\\\\tresult\\\\n' >> \\\"$logfile\\\"\\nfi\\n\\nts=\\\"$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)\\\"\\n# Record separators were rejected above. Explains subsystem architecture, runtime flow, onboarding mental models. Use why for motivation.\\\"\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\n---\\n\\n# How\\n\\nExplore the codebase to answer \\\"how does X work?\\\" questions. Produce architectural explanations at the level of a senior engineer onboarding onto a subsystem, enough to build a working mental model, not so much that it reads like annotated source code.\\n\\nBefore dispatch, read [session capabilities](../../references/host-capabilities.md), [model roles](../../references/model-roles.md), and the [assignment contract](../../references/orchestration-contract.md). Bind worker operations to tools actually exposed and authorized in this session. Request the inherited parent model and effort unless a supported explicit selection is observed. Retain rejections and disclose replacements; an unavailable required selection is blocked. Record requested and observed selections separately, using unknown for unobserved values.\\n\\nKeep explorers and explainers read-only. Worker assignments record their role, distinct angle, exact input revision, identity and inspected results under the assignment contract. Reading a prompt does not register a worker. If independent workers are unavailable or unauthorized, disclose reduced capability and perform the same exploration and explanation roles sequentially. Never claim parallel or independent exploration from sequential work. If source access is unavailable or denied, report the gap and limit the explanation to inspected evidence.\\n\\n## Step 1. Assess Complexity\\n\\nIf the scope is ambiguous, state your interpretation and explore. The user can redirect.\\n\\n- **Simple** (a single module, a small utility, a narrow question such as \\\"how does function X work\\\"): no explorers. One explainer explores and explains in a single pass. Go to Step 2b.\\n- **Complex** (a subsystem spanning multiple files or services, a cross-cutting feature, a full architectural overview): use parallel explorers when available, then hand off to the explainer. Go to Step 2a.\\n\\nWhen in doubt, take the simple path.\\n\\n## Step 2a. Explore (complex questions only)\\n\\nDecompose the question into 2 to 4 exploration angles, each a distinct slice of the subsystem. Dispatch all explorers together through an observed worker binding, with distinct assignments:\\n\\n- Role: how explorer\\n- Model and effort: follow the model-role contract\\n- Access: read-only\\n\\nEach explorer gets the prompt in `references/explorer-prompt.md` with its angle filled in. If workers are unavailable, explore those distinct angles sequentially and retain separate findings. Then go to Step 3.\\n\\n## Step 2b. Direct Explain (simple questions)\\n\\nAssign one explainer worker that explores and explains in one pass:\\n\\n- Role: how explainer\\n- Model and effort: follow the model-role contract\\n- Access: read-only\\n\\nBuild its prompt from `references/explainer-prompt.md` without the explorer-findings section. The explainer reads and traces the source itself. If workers are unavailable, apply this role sequentially. Go to Step 4.\\n\\n## Step 3. Synthesize (complex questions only)\\n\\nOnce all explorer results have been inspected, assign one explainer worker to synthesize their findings into one explanation:\\n\\n- Role: how explainer\\n- Model and effort: follow the model-role contract\\n- Access: read-only\\n\\nBuild its prompt from `references/explainer-prompt.md` with every explorer's findings filled in. In reduced capability, synthesize the sequential findings under the same read-only role.\\n\\n## Step 4. Present\\n\\nPresent the explainer's output to the user. Light edits for clarity or context from the conversation are fine. Do not substantially rewrite it.\\n\\n## Output Format\\n\\nThe explanation uses the sections defined in `references/explainer-prompt.md`, dropping any that do not apply: Overview, Key Concepts, How It Works, Where Things Live, Gotchas.\\n# Explorer Prompt Template\\n\\nBuild each explorer worker's prompt from this template. Fill in the placeholders.\\n\\n---\\n\\nYou are exploring a codebase to understand how something works. Gather facts. Trace code paths, read implementations, map components. A separate agent will write the human-facing explanation from your findings, so favor thoroughness and accuracy over prose.\\n\\nWhen independent workers are available, other explorers investigate different slices in parallel. In reduced capability, the coordinator explores distinct slices sequentially and discloses that limit. Don't try to cover everything. Focus on your assigned angle and go deep.\\n\\n## Question\\n\\n> {QUESTION}\\n\\n## Your Exploration Angle\\n\\n{EXPLORATION_ANGLE}\\n\\n## Exploration Instructions\\n\\nStart by finding the relevant code. Use available file discovery, symbol search and file-reading tools to understand the actual implementation. Don't guess from names. Read the code.\\n\\nFollow this pattern:\\n1. **Find the entry point.** What triggers this behavior? A user action, an API call, a scheduled job? Find where it starts.\\n2. **Trace the flow.** Follow the call chain from the entry point. Read each function. Understand what data flows through and how it transforms.\\n3. **Map the key abstractions.** What types, interfaces, services, or classes are central? Read their definitions. Understand what they represent and why they exist.\\n4. **Find the boundaries.** Where does this subsystem interface with others? What goes in, what comes out?\\n5. **Look for the non-obvious.** Anything surprising? Anything that looks like a historical artifact? Anything a newcomer would misunderstand?\\n\\nKeep exploring until you can describe the full picture without hand-waving. If you hit a part you can't trace, say so explicitly. \\\"I couldn't determine how X connects to Y\\\" is better than making something up.\\n\\n## Output\\n\\nReturn your findings in this structure. Be factual and specific. Reference exact file paths, function names, type names, and line numbers where relevant.\\n\\n### Components Found\\nThe key types, services, classes, and abstractions. For each: name, file path, and a one-sentence description of what it does.\\n\\n### Flow\\nThe execution flow step by step. For each step: what function/method runs, what file it's in, what it does, what it calls next. Include the data that flows between steps.\\n\\n### Files Read\\nEvery file you read during exploration, so the explainer can reference them.\\n\\n### Boundaries\\nWhere this subsystem connects to other parts of the codebase. The inputs and outputs.\\n\\n### Non-Obvious Things\\nAnything surprising, historically motivated, or easy to get wrong. Things that look like they should work one way but work another.\\n\\n### Open Questions\\nAnything you couldn't fully trace or understand. Be honest about gaps.\\n# Explainer Prompt Template\\n\\nBuild the explainer worker's prompt from this template. Fill in the placeholders.\\n\\n---\\n\\nYou are writing an architectural explanation for a senior engineer. For complex questions, explorers have traced different slices and gathered findings, independently when supported or sequentially with an explicit reduced-capability disclosure. For simple questions, omit Explorer Findings and explore the source yourself in this role. Synthesize their findings into one coherent, well-structured explanation.\\n\\n## Original Question\\n\\n> {QUESTION}\\n\\n## Explorer Findings\\n\\n{EXPLORER_FINDINGS_ALL}\\n\\n## Instructions\\n\\nThe explorers each investigated a different angle of the same subsystem. Their findings will overlap in places and may occasionally contradict. Reconcile them. Merge overlapping descriptions, resolve contradictions by checking the code yourself, and combine the separate slices into a unified picture.\\n\\nWrite an explanation a senior engineer unfamiliar with this area could read and walk away with a solid mental model, understanding the architecture well enough to start working in it confidently.\\n\\nYou have read-only access to the codebase to check anything, clarify a detail, or fill a gap. Use available file reading, symbol search and file discovery as needed. When explorer findings are supplied, you should not need to re-explore from scratch. Without them, trace entry points, calls, data, abstractions and boundaries yourself; disclose anything you cannot trace.\\n\\n## Output Format\\n\\nUse this structure, adapted to what makes sense for the question. Not every section is needed for every question.\\n\\n### Overview\\n1-2 paragraphs. What is this thing, what does it do, why does it exist. Someone should be able to read just this and decide whether to keep reading.\\n\\n### Key Concepts\\nThe important types, services, or abstractions needed to follow the rest. Brief definitions, not exhaustive.\\n\\n### How It Works\\nThe core of the explanation, and the longest section. Walk through the flow: what triggers it, what happens step by step, where data goes, what the decision points are.\\n\\nUse prose, not pseudocode. Reference specific files and functions so the reader knows where to look, but don't dump large code blocks unless a snippet is essential to a point.\\n\\nWhen the flow involves multiple components talking to each other, or data transforming through stages, include a diagram. Use mermaid (```mermaid) for structured flows (sequence diagrams, flowcharts, component graphs) or ASCII art for simpler relationships where mermaid would be overkill. Use your judgment. A diagram should clarify, not decorate. If prose covers the flow, skip the diagram.\\n\\n### Where Things Live\\nA brief file/directory map. Just the ones someone would need to start working here.\\n\\n### Gotchas\\nNon-obvious things, surprising behavior, historical context, pitfalls. Skip this section if there's nothing worth calling out.\\n\\n## Communication Style\\n\\n- Use concrete language, not abstractions-about-abstractions\\n- Say \\\"the `UserService` calls `AuthClient.refresh()`\\\" not \\\"the service delegates to the client\\\"\\n- When something is complex, explain why it's complex. Don't just describe the complexity\\n- When something is simple, don't pad it out\\n- If there's a helpful analogy, use it. If there isn't, don't force one\\n- If the explorers flagged open questions or gaps, acknowledge them rather than hiding them\\n---\\nname: why\\ndescription: \\\"Use for 'why does X work this way', 'why we picked Y', design rationale, regressions, postmortems, or data-backed thresholds. Discovers available MCPs and queries each evidence category (source control, issue tracker, long-form docs, real-time chat, infrastructure observability, error tracking, product analytics warehouse) in parallel, then returns a cited read on decisions and tradeoffs. Use how for runtime behavior.\\\"\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\n---\\n\\n# Why\\n\\nInvestigate the motivation and intent behind code.\\n\\nCompanion to the `how` skill. `how` answers what the code does and how it works. `why` answers what forces led to its shape.\\n\\nRead [host capabilities](../../references/host-capabilities.md), [model roles](../../references/model-roles.md), and the [orchestration contract](../../references/orchestration-contract.md) before assigning investigators. Bind operations to tools exposed in this session and observe results. Preserve the role labels `why investigators` and `why synthesizer`; select supported models under the model-role contract. Record requested and actual models only when observed, otherwise use `unknown`. Invocation metadata above is retained without assuming host enforcement.\\n\\n## Operating Posture\\n\\nOperate as a **careful, cautious, and precise investigator**. Be honest about what you know vs what you're inferring. Read `references/epistemics.md` for the full confidence framework and phrasing guide. The synthesizer must follow it.\\n\\n## Step 1. Understand the Target and the Question\\n\\nParse what the user is asking. The **target** is usually a chunk of code, a pattern, a feature, or a named design decision. The **question** is usually a design rationale, a tradeoff, a motivating edge case, an external constraint, dead code, or a broad history sweep.\\n\\nIf the target is vague (\\\"why do we do it this way?\\\" with no clear referent), make your best guess from conversation context (open files, recent edits, cursor location, what was just discussed). State your interpretation briefly so the user can redirect if you're off, then proceed.\\n\\n## Step 2. Establish the Code Anchor\\n\\nBefore spawning investigators, anchor the investigation in concrete code. You need:\\n\\n- The relevant file path(s) and line range(s)\\n- The key symbols (function names, class names, constants)\\n- An initial commit list. The last few commits touching the target.\\n- PR numbers from merge commits (pattern `(#1234)` in the subject line)\\n\\nBuild this inline.\\n\\n```bash\\n# Blame target lines for last-touch commits\\ngit blame -L <start>,<end> <file>\\n\\n# Full file history, with patches, through renames\\ngit log --follow -p -- <file>\\n\\n# Last N commits touching the file, PR numbers visible\\ngit log --oneline -20 -- <file>\\n\\n# Extract PR numbers from a commit message\\ngit log -1 --format=%B <commit>\\n```\\n\\nPull PR bodies and discussion via `gh` for any substantive commits:\\n\\n```bash\\ngh pr view <number> --json title,body,author,createdAt,mergedAt,labels,closingIssuesReferences,comments,reviews\\n```\\n\\nCapture this as seed context (file paths, symbols, commits, PR numbers, linked ticket IDs). Pass it to the investigators.\\n\\n## Step 3. Spawn Parallel Investigators (default posture)\\n\\n**Default to the full parallel investigation.**\\n\\n### Discovery\\n\\nBefore spawning investigators, inspect the session’s exposed tools and connector descriptions. Do not assume a host-specific MCP directory exists. Discover read operations, authorization and observed access for each category. Source-specific API names in the playbooks are examples; bind their purpose to the actual tool schema before use.\\n\\nMap each available MCP to one evidence category:\\n\\n1. Source control history\\n2. Issue / ticket tracker\\n3. Long-form documents\\n4. Real-time team chat\\n5. Infrastructure observability\\n6. Error / exception tracking\\n7. Product analytics warehouse\\n\\nTry authorized local git history and available `gh` or source-control connector reads. Neither execution nor authenticated PR access is guaranteed. Keep local history and shared PR records distinct, and report missing access explicitly. For the other six, classify using the MCP name, server instructions, tool names, and resource descriptors. If an MCP could fit more than one category, choose the one matching its primary evidence. Record ambiguous cases in the coverage map.\\n\\nAim for a complete **coverage map**. Document unavailable, denied, failed and searched-empty categories separately. An unavailable source is not a null search result.\\n\\nLaunch all matching investigators in a single message so they run concurrently. Don't ask one agent to cover multiple MCPs.\\n\\nInvestigator configuration follows the orchestration contract. Each investigator owns one source, uses the `why investigators` role, and needs authorized source reads. A host mode that strips connectors cannot serve a connector-backed investigation. Keep investigators read-only in behavior: do not write files, send messages, change tickets, authenticate accounts, or modify external state. If independent workers are unavailable, perform separately scoped sequential category passes and synthesis, label reduced capability, and never claim worker independence. If no authorized source reads remain, report blocked.\\n\\nEach investigator gets:\\n1. The base prompt from `references/investigator-prompt.md`\\n2. The category playbook `references/sources/<source>.md` for the selected MCP, adapted from the examples in `references/source-playbook.md`\\n3. The cross-cutting `references/sources/incident-postmortem.md` **if the target code looks defensive** (null checks, retry logic, timeout handling, rate limiting, feature flags, egress guards, OOM handlers)\\n4. The code anchor from Step 2 (file paths, symbols, commit hashes, PR numbers, ticket IDs)\\n5. The user's original question\\n\\n### Investigator roster. One per available evidence category\\n\\nSpawn one investigator per category that has a matching MCP. Each owns exactly one tool or MCP.\\n\\nEach entry names the category and the kind of \\\"why\\\" it uniquely surfaces. Use it to know what to expect back, how to name a gap when a category returns empty, and (only in the rare provably-irrelevant case) to justify a skip.\\n\\n1. **Source control investigator**. Git history, `gh` for PRs, code comments, tests. Always attempt this category. Missing git, execution or PR access is a gap. Best at surfacing *implementation-time rationale captured during review*.\\n\\n2. **Issue / ticket tracker investigator** (e.g. Linear, Jira, GitHub Issues, Plane, Shortcut MCP). Best at surfacing *the product or business forcing function*. Strongest when the why is external to engineering.\\n\\n3. **Long-form documents investigator** (e.g. Notion, Confluence, Google Docs, Coda MCP). Best at surfacing *long-form design rationale*. Where the why is written out before it becomes code.\\n\\n4. **Real-time team chat investigator** (e.g. Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams, Mattermost MCP). Best at surfacing *real-time deliberation that never reached a doc*. Especially important when the source control, ticket, and doc paper trail is thin.\\n\\n5. **Infrastructure observability investigator** (e.g. Datadog, New Relic, Honeycomb, Grafana, Splunk MCP). Infra/runtime view. Best at surfacing *infrastructure and runtime reality that motivated the code*. Strongest when the target reacts to an infra signal (timeouts, retries, rate limits, circuit breakers).\\n\\n6. **Error / exception tracking investigator** (e.g. Sentry, Rollbar, Bugsnag, Airbrake MCP). Best at surfacing *the specific exceptions and error trajectories that motivated defensive or corrective code*. Strongest for catch blocks, null guards, type checks, retries, and other defenses.\\n\\n7. **Product analytics warehouse investigator** (e.g. Databricks, Snowflake, BigQuery, ClickHouse, dbt, Redshift MCP). Product/data view. Best at surfacing *product and data reality that shaped the code*. Strongest for flag-gated code, experiment-driven ships, data migrations, and \\\"where did this number come from\\\" questions.\\n\\n### When to skip an investigator\\n\\nOnly skip with an **explicit, written justification** that goes in the final \\\"Sources Consulted\\\" section. Two valid reasons:\\n\\n- **No MCP is available for that category** in this environment. Flag this as a gap, not a choice. Example: \\\"Real-time team chat skipped. No matching MCP available, so the conversational record was not searchable.\\\"\\n- **The source is provably irrelevant**, not just \\\"probably irrelevant.\\\" A high bar. Example: \\\"Error / exception tracking skipped. Target is a build-time script with no runtime code path.\\\"\\n\\nIf your scope assessment suggests a single-commit trivial target where the PR description already contains the complete answer, you may answer inline **only after** confirming all seven available category searches would be redundant. Say so explicitly. This should be rare.\\n\\n## Step 4. Synthesize\\n\\nSpawn one synthesizer through an observed worker binding, using the `why synthesizer` role and authorized source reads for citation checks. Use sequential synthesis with an explicit reduced-capability label when workers are unavailable. The synthesizer must not write files or modify external state.\\n\\nThe synthesizer gets:\\n1. The investigator findings, including any null results and any categories skipped with justification\\n2. The code anchor from Step 2 (file paths, symbols, commit hashes, PR numbers, ticket IDs)\\n3. The user's original question\\n4. The epistemics framework from `references/epistemics.md`\\n5. The synthesizer prompt template from `references/synthesizer-prompt.md`\\n\\n## Step 5. Present\\n\\nTake the synthesizer's output and present it to the user. You may lightly edit for clarity or add context from the conversation, but **do not rewrite the confidence language**.\\n\\n## Output Format\\n\\nThe output structure is the one in `references/synthesizer-prompt.md`: The Question, The Code in Question, What We Found, What We Can Reasonably Infer, Competing Hypotheses, What We Don't Know, Sources Consulted, Confidence Summary. Adapt as needed, but keep the confidence separation intact, and keep Sources Consulted as one line per investigator, including the ones that returned nothing or were skipped, with the reason.\\n\\nAfter the Sources Consulted block, if the user's `why` question is a precursor to actually changing this code, convert the lineage findings into a Preserve / Change / Avoid / Risk constraint set suitable for planning the change.\\n\\n## Common Failure Modes to Avoid\\n\\n- **Recency bias**. Assuming the most recent commit is authoritative. The current shape is often the accretion of many earlier decisions. Trace back.\\n\\nKeep private source visibility intact. Retrieve only authorized relevant content, avoid raw telemetry or personal-data dumps, and do not redistribute restricted records beyond the authorized audience. External messages and writes require separate explicit authorization.\\n\\n## Reference Files\\n\\n- `references/epistemics.md`. Confidence tiers and phrasing guide. The synthesizer must follow it.\\n- `references/investigator-prompt.md`. Base prompt template for investigator subagents.\\n- `references/source-playbook.md`. Index pointing at the category playbooks below.\\n- `references/sources/*.md`. One self-contained example playbook per category, plus cross-cutting `incident-postmortem.md`. Give an investigator the single file that matches its category and adapt it to the available MCP.\\n- `references/synthesizer-prompt.md`. Prompt template for the synthesizer subagent, including the output format.\\n# Investigator Prompt Template\\n\\nBuild each investigator's prompt from this template. Fill in the placeholders. Append the single category playbook `sources/<source>.md` matching this investigator's evidence category (see `source-playbook.md` for the index). If the target code looks defensive (null checks, retry logic, timeout handling, rate limiting, feature flags, egress guards, OOM handlers), also append `sources/incident-postmortem.md` for the incident-flavored queries to run inside its own source.\\n\\n---\\n\\nYou are investigating the historical context and motivation behind a piece of code. A separate synthesizer combines your findings with other investigators' into a final answer, so gather evidence accurately rather than writing prose.\\n\\nOther investigators search different sources in parallel. Don't try to cover everything. Focus on your assigned source and go deep.\\n\\n## Operating Posture\\n\\nWork like a careful, cautious, precise investigator. Don't produce a narrative. Surface evidence and describe it accurately, including the parts that don't fit a tidy story. The more boring and exact your output, the more useful it is. A single verbatim quote with a precise citation beats a paragraph of plausible-sounding summary.\\n\\n- **Quote, don't paraphrase** when the exact wording matters. Citations should let the reader jump to the source and confirm the claim in seconds.\\n- **Go wide before going deep.** Cast a broad first net so you don't miss related context. Only then narrow in.\\n- **Track what you searched, not just what you found.** An absence is only useful if the reader knows what was looked for. Record queries verbatim.\\n- **Resist the story.** If three pieces of evidence line up neatly and a fourth contradicts them, the contradiction is the most interesting finding. Don't file it away.\\n- **Consider the counterfactual.** Before reporting a finding as strong, ask whether you would expect to find it if your current reading were wrong, and how the evidence would differ.\\n- **Never invent.** If you're tempted to round a partial finding up into a confident statement, stop and label it partial. The synthesizer is counting on your output being accurate.\\n\\n## The Question\\n\\n> {QUESTION}\\n\\n## The Code Anchor\\n\\n**Target files:** {FILES_WITH_LINE_RANGES}\\n\\n**Key symbols:** {SYMBOLS}\\n\\n**Initial commits touching this code (most recent first):**\\n{COMMIT_LIST}\\n\\n**PR numbers extracted from commit messages:** {PR_NUMBERS}\\n\\n**Ticket IDs mentioned in commits or PR bodies (if any):** {TICKET_IDS}\\n\\n## Your Assigned Source\\n\\n{SOURCE_NAME}\\n\\n{SOURCE_PLAYBOOK_SECTION}\\n\\n## Investigation Instructions\\n\\nGather **evidence**. Don't answer the question directly. The synthesizer weighs the evidence and forms conclusions. Follow this loop:\\n\\n1. **Cast a wide net first.** Start broad so you don't miss related context, then narrow in on specific items.\\n2. **Read the whole thing.** Read any PR, ticket, doc, or thread fully, not just the title or summary. The key evidence is often buried in a comment, a subtask, or a follow-up.\\n3. **Follow links within your assigned source.** If a PR references another PR or commit, pull it. If a ticket links a parent or sibling, pull it. If a doc links another doc, pull it. Stay inside your assigned source. When you spot a cross-source reference, do NOT chase it yourself. Record it under \\\"Additional Leads\\\" so the investigator assigned to that source can pick it up. The one-investigator-per-category design depends on this. Chasing cross-source links duplicates work and confuses scope.\\n4. **Capture quotes verbatim** with their location (PR number, ticket ID, URL, commit hash, file:line). The synthesizer needs to cite this precisely.\\n5. **Note absences.** If you searched for something and came up empty, that's also a finding. Record what you searched for and what you didn't find.\\n6. **Watch for contradictions.** If two items in your source disagree, record both. Don't suppress the inconvenient one.\\n\\nDon't synthesize or form a final opinion on \\\"the why.\\\" Collect the raw material honestly and completely. The synthesizer does the reasoning.\\n\\n## Epistemic Discipline\\n\\n- **Don't confuse mechanics with motivation.** A commit changing `limit = 50` to `limit = 100` shows the change, not necessarily why. Look for the explanation in the commit message, PR description, linked ticket, or review comments.\\n- **Don't infer intent from code style.** \\\"The author chose a functional approach\\\" is an observation about code, not evidence of intent. Claim intent only when the author stated it.\\n- **Preserve uncertainty.** If the evidence is ambiguous, say so. If one reading is more plausible but not certain, say that. Don't collapse ambiguity to look decisive.\\n- **No silent substitutions.** If the question is about feature X and you only find evidence about feature Y, don't present Y's evidence as if it answers X.\\n\\n## Output Format\\n\\nReturn your findings in this structure. The synthesizer will read it directly.\\n\\n### Source\\nWhich source you investigated (source control, issue / ticket tracker, long-form documents, real-time team chat, infrastructure observability, error / exception tracking, product analytics warehouse, code comments, etc.).\\n\\n### What I Searched\\nThe queries you ran, the items you opened, the places you looked. Be specific. This tells the synthesizer how thorough the investigation was and what might still be unsearched.\\n\\n### Direct Evidence Found\\nFor each piece that explicitly addresses the question:\\n- **What it says**: verbatim quote or accurate paraphrase\\n- **Where it's from**: PR #123, ticket ID, doc URL, chat permalink, commit hash, or file:line\\n- **Author and date** (if available)\\n- **Relevance**: one sentence on how it bears on the question\\n\\n### Indirect / Circumstantial Evidence\\nItems that don't explicitly answer the question but bear on it. For each:\\n- **What it is**: brief description\\n- **Where it's from**: location\\n- **What it suggests**: what a careful reader might infer, and why. Name the inference chain.\\n- **Alternative readings**: if the same evidence could support a different interpretation, note it\\n\\n### Contradictions\\nTwo items that disagree with each other, with both citations.\\n\\n### Gaps\\nWhat you searched for and didn't find. Be specific: \\\"Searched the issue tracker for [query] across [time range]. No matching issues.\\\" These absences are valuable data.\\n\\n### Additional Leads\\nAnything that suggests further investigation in a different source. For example, if a PR references a chat thread that wasn't in your source, note it so the real-time team chat investigator or a follow-up pass can pursue it.\\n\\n## What You're Not Doing\\n\\n- Writing the final answer. The synthesizer does that.\\n- Picking sides in contradictions. Surface them.\\n- Speculating beyond what the evidence supports. A hunch with no evidence isn't evidence.\\n- Reading the code itself to figure out intent. You may read the code to understand what the target *is*, but don't confuse \\\"what the code does\\\" with \\\"why.\\\"\\n# Synthesizer Prompt Template\\n\\nBuild the synthesizer's prompt from this template. Fill in the placeholders.\\n\\n---\\n\\nYou are answering a \\\"why\\\" question about a piece of code by synthesizing findings from multiple investigators who searched different historical sources (source control, issue / ticket tracker, long-form documents, real-time team chat, infrastructure observability, error / exception tracking, product analytics warehouse, and code comments). Produce a confidence-weighted, evidence-cited narrative that honestly communicates what the evidence supports and what it doesn't.\\n\\n## The Question\\n\\n> {QUESTION}\\n\\n## The Code Anchor\\n\\n**Target files:** {FILES_WITH_LINE_RANGES}\\n\\n**Key symbols:** {SYMBOLS}\\n\\n## Investigator Findings\\n\\n{ALL_INVESTIGATOR_FINDINGS}\\n\\n## Sources That Weren't Searched\\n\\n{SKIPPED_SOURCES_WITH_REASONS}\\n\\n## Epistemics Framework\\n\\nYou MUST follow the framework in `references/epistemics.md`. Read it in full before writing the output. The key rules:\\n\\n1. Every claim sits in one of these tiers: **Direct**, **Supported**, **Inferred**, **Speculative**, **Unknown**. The tier determines what section the claim goes in and how it's phrased.\\n2. Every Direct/Supported claim must have a citation (PR #, ticket ID, doc URL, chat permalink, commit hash, or file:line).\\n3. Inferred and Speculative claims must use hedged language (\\\"appears to\\\", \\\"likely\\\", \\\"suggests\\\", \\\"one possibility is\\\").\\n4. Never cite code as evidence for its own intent.\\n5. Gaps in the evidence must be documented. Don't fill them with plausible-sounding guesses.\\n6. If the user's question embedded a hypothesis, treat it as a candidate, not a conclusion. Check the evidence independently.\\n\\n## Instructions\\n\\n1. **Read all investigator findings.** They gathered raw evidence, not conclusions. You weigh it.\\n2. **Reconcile overlapping findings.** Multiple investigators may have cited the same PR, ticket, or doc. Merge into a single, authoritative reference.\\n3. **Identify contradictions.** If two items of evidence disagree, don't pick one. Surface both.\\n4. **Calibrate confidence.** For each claim, identify the evidence and the tier. State Direct claims plainly with a citation. Hedge Inferred claims and explain the inference. Mark Speculative claims explicitly. Put claims with no evidence in the gaps section.\\n5. **Verify citations by spot-checking.** You can read the codebase and call MCP tools to verify citations. Do not write files, commit, or modify external state. If you're uncertain a cited item exists or says what's claimed, check it. Don't propagate errors.\\n6. **Don't overreach.** The user will act on your output. Better to leave an open question open than to fill it with a confident-sounding guess.\\n\\n## Output Format\\n\\nWrite the output for the user. Use this exact structure:\\n\\n---\\n\\n### The Question\\n\\nRestate the user's question in one or two sentences so the answer is anchored.\\n\\n### The Code in Question\\n\\nFile paths, line ranges, key symbols. Two or three lines to orient a reader who lands here cold.\\n\\n### What We Found\\n\\n**Claims with direct evidence**, one per bullet. Quote or paraphrase the source and cite precisely. Format each finding like:\\n\\n```markdown\\n- **[Direct]** {Claim}. Source: [PR #123](url) / ticket ID / file:line. {Brief quote or paraphrase.}\\n- **[Supported]** {Claim}. Evidence: {list of items and what each contributes}.\\n```\\n\\nUse `[Direct]` for single-source, explicit evidence. Use `[Supported]` when multiple indirect items converge on a conclusion.\\n\\n### What We Can Reasonably Infer\\n\\n**Claims that aren't explicitly stated anywhere but are well-supported by indirect evidence.** Make the inference chain visible: \\\"Given A and B, it's likely that C.\\\" Use hedged language (\\\"appears to\\\", \\\"likely\\\", \\\"suggests\\\", \\\"is consistent with\\\"). Format:\\n\\n- **[Inferred]** {Hedged claim}. Reasoning: {the specific evidence and the inference step}.\\n\\nIf there's nothing to infer, skip this section.\\n\\n### Competing Hypotheses\\n\\n**If the evidence fits multiple stories, present them.** Don't force a winner when the record doesn't support one. For each hypothesis:\\n\\n- **Hypothesis:** {one-sentence statement}\\n- **Evidence for:** {specific items}\\n- **Evidence against or missing:** {what would need to be true but isn't, or what counter-signals exist}\\n\\nSkip this section if there's a single clear answer.\\n\\n### What We Don't Know\\n\\n**Explicit gaps.** Things the user asked that the evidence didn't answer. Sources searched that came up empty. Sources that weren't searchable at all, such as a missing real-time team chat MCP.\\n\\nBe specific. \\\"We searched the issue tracker for [query1], [query2], [query3] and found no issue discussing the rate-limit threshold\\\" is useful. \\\"We don't know why\\\" is not. Include:\\n\\n- Specific questions that went unanswered\\n- Searches that returned nothing\\n- Sources that were unavailable (and why)\\n- People who would likely know but who you can't ask\\n\\n### Sources Consulted\\n\\nBulleted list of what was actually searched, so the user can judge coverage and redirect. Format:\\n\\n- **Source control history**: {file paths}, {number of commits reviewed}, PRs #{numbers}, and code comments searched. Or \\\"Not searched. Git history, command execution or authenticated PR access was unavailable or denied; name the exact gap.\\\"\\n- **Issue / ticket tracker**: {ticket IDs and keyword searches}. Or \\\"Not searched. No matching MCP available in this environment.\\\"\\n- **Long-form documents**: {page titles and search queries}. Or \\\"Not searched. No matching MCP available in this environment.\\\"\\n- **Real-time team chat**: {channels searched, date ranges, queries}. Or \\\"Not searched. No matching MCP available in this environment.\\\"\\n- **Infrastructure observability**: {dashboards, monitors, metrics, logs, traces, or incidents searched}. Or \\\"Not searched. No matching MCP available in this environment.\\\"\\n- **Error / exception tracking**: {issues, events, or releases searched}. Or \\\"Not searched. No matching MCP available in this environment.\\\"\\n- **Product analytics warehouse**: {fully-qualified tables queried, the time windows, and the numeric summaries (counts, percentiles, first/last-seen timestamps) that bore on the question}. Or \\\"Not searched. No matching MCP available in this environment.\\\"\\n\\n### Confidence Summary\\n\\nOne or two sentences summarizing your overall confidence. E.g.:\\n\\n> \\\"The core rationale (A) is well-supported by direct PR and ticket evidence. The specific threshold value (100) is inferred from the surrounding context but not explicitly documented. The question of whether this was driven by a customer request could not be answered. No relevant issue tracker or long-form doc content surfaced, and real-time team chat search was unavailable.\\\"\\n\\n---\\n\\n## Quality Check Before Returning\\n\\nBefore finalizing, review your output against this checklist:\\n\\n1. Does every claim in \\\"What We Found\\\" have a citation? If not, add one or move the claim to \\\"Inferred\\\" or \\\"Hypotheses.\\\"\\n2. Is the phrasing tier-appropriate? (Direct claims can use \\\"because\\\". Inferred claims cannot.)\\n3. Did you surface any contradictions you noticed, or did you quietly pick one?\\n4. Does the \\\"What We Don't Know\\\" section exist and name specific gaps? If it's empty or missing, be suspicious. Historical investigations almost always have gaps.\\n5. If the user embedded a hypothesis in their question, did you check it against the evidence rather than rubber-stamping it?\\n6. Did you cite any code as evidence for its own intent? Remove those. Code is mechanics, not motivation.\\n7. Is the overall tone calibrated? A confident-sounding answer with weak evidence is the exact failure mode this skill exists to prevent.\\n\\nIf any item fails, revise before returning.\\n\\n## A Final Note\\n\\nThe value of this output comes from its honesty, not its authority. A reader who takes your answer to the original author, an engineering lead, or a product manager should be well-positioned to ask the right follow-up questions. Be clear about what's known, what's inferred, and what's missing. Don't optimize for looking decisive. Optimize for being useful.\\n\"\n  }\n}\n"

      "sha256": "579eb53be003439dadb21350097654d12f35dcc9e66d421014ef246d9f77d06c",

      "text": "{\n  \"request\": {\n    \"cmd\": \"cat /root/.codex/plugins/cache/created-by-me-remote/pstack-openai/0.1.3/skills/principle-build-the-lever/SKILL.md /root/.codex/plugins/cache/created-by-me-remote/pstack-openai/0.1.3/skills/principle-guard-the-context-window/SKILL.md /root/.codex/plugins/cache/created-by-me-remote/pstack-openai/0.1.3/skills/principle-sequence-verifiable-units/SKILL.md /root/.codex/plugins/cache/created-by-me-remote/pstack-openai/0.1.3/references/agent-prompts/poteto-agent.md; date -u +%FT%TZ\",\n    \"max_output_tokens\": 7000\n  },\n  \"returned\": {\n    \"chunk_id\": \"faabc3\",\n    \"wall_time_seconds\": 0.000038768,\n    \"exit_code\": 0,\n    \"original_token_count\": 2331,\n    \"output\": \"---\\nname: principle-build-the-lever\\ndescription: \\\"Apply to any non-trivial work, not just bulk work: edits, migrations, analyses, checks. Build the tool that does it or proves it (codemod, script, generator, or a skill your subagents follow) instead of working by hand. The tool is the artifact a reviewer can rerun.\\\"\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\n---\\n# Build the Lever\\n\\nWhen the work isn't trivial, build the tool that does it instead of doing it by hand.\\n\\n**Why:** Two payoffs. Throughput: a codemod, generator, or script does the work the same way every time and reruns for free. Confidence: the tool is one artifact a reviewer can read and rerun to check the work. Hand-done changes can only be re-verified by redoing them. A deterministic script turns \\\"trust me\\\" into \\\"run this\\\".\\n\\n**Pattern:** Default to building the lever. Skip it only when the task is trivial, a couple of obvious edits you can see at a glance.\\n\\n- Do the first unit by hand to learn the recipe, then build the tool. Prove it by rerunning it on that unit and diffing against your hand-done version. Make the lever safe to rerun.\\n- Codemod or script for edits, generator for repetitive files, a dump-to-sqlite query for analysis, a rerunnable check for verification.\\n- A deterministic lever beats fan-out. If the tool can process every unit in one pass, run it yourself. Don't fan out delegates to hand-apply what a script can do.\\n- When you fan work out to subagents, write the lever as a skill they all read: the recipe, the verification contract, and the do-not-touch fences in one artifact. Keep it outside the delegates' write scope so they can't quietly edit the contract.\\n- Applying this principle produces a file. If you cited it and there is no codemod, script, generator, or delegate skill in the diff, you didn't apply it.\\n- Commit the lever when the work outlives the session.\\n\\n**Balance:** The bar is triviality, not repetition. A one-off still earns a lever when the lever is what makes the work checkable. Per the [Laziness Protocol](../principle-laziness-protocol/SKILL.md), build the smallest script that does or proves the job, never a framework.\\n\\nDistinct from [Encode Lessons in Structure](../principle-encode-lessons-in-structure/SKILL.md), which makes a recurring instruction a durable guardrail. This is throughput and reviewability on the work in front of you. For scripting the verification itself, see [Prove It Works](../principle-prove-it-works/SKILL.md).\\n\\n## Host capability and permission boundaries\\n\\nUse the [host capability contract](../../references/host-capabilities.md) to discover file reads, authorized writes, execution and persistence. A proposed tool is not a saved artifact. A saved artifact is not executed proof. Report the commands, exit status and comparisons you observed; if execution is denied or unavailable, state that proof is blocked and provide the proposed rerun and diff procedure as reduced capability. If source reads are unavailable, do not claim a verified recipe.\\n\\nDelegation requires user authorization and exposed independent-worker operations under the [orchestration contract](../../references/orchestration-contract.md). Keep the shared recipe outside worker write scopes. Sequential work is reduced capability and never proves independent workers. Preserve the [active workflow owner](../../references/workflow-ownership.md).\\n\\nRetaining the lever beyond the session does not grant commit permission. Commit only when authorized. Do not install dependencies, publish or perform external writes as incidental steps. Preserve `disable-model-invocation: true` metadata without assuming the host enforces it.\\n---\\nname: principle-guard-the-context-window\\ndescription: \\\"Apply when context is filling up: large outputs, long files, repeated reads, fan-out planning. Route bulk to subagents; keep summaries in the main thread, not raw payloads.\\\"\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\n---\\n\\n# Guard the Context Window\\n\\nThe context window is finite and non-renewable within a session. Every token should be worth its cost.\\n\\n**Why:** Context overflow degrades reasoning quality, creates compression artifacts, and halts progress.\\n\\n**Pattern:**\\n- **Isolate large payloads.** Route verbose outputs, screenshots, and large documents to subagents. The main context gets summaries, not raw data.\\n- **Keep frequently used content inline.** Templates and references used on every invocation belong in the skill file, not in separate files that cost a read each time.\\n- **Size phases and cap scope.** Limit files per phase, set turn budgets, account for mechanism costs.\\n\\n## Capability and permission boundaries\\n\\nUse the [session capability contract](../../references/host-capabilities.md) to check evidence access and independent-worker operations. Delegate only when the task authorizes it and the session exposes those operations. Follow the [assignment and integration contract](../../references/orchestration-contract.md), retain observed worker identities and inspect their results before reporting summaries. This principle grants no additional permissions.\\n\\nIf independent workers are unavailable or unauthorized, narrow accessible evidence into bounded sequential phases. Keep summaries in the main thread and label this reduced capability. Sequential work does not establish worker independence. If required evidence is inaccessible, name the missing input and access limit; keep the plan provisional and do not claim to have read or summarized it.\\n\\nPreserve the invocation metadata above without assuming the host enforces it. Report delegation and inspection only after observing the authorized operations.\\n---\\nname: principle-sequence-verifiable-units\\ndescription: \\\"Apply to multi-step work (sweeps, migrations, runs of similar edits) and to how you stack commits and PRs. Break work into small units that each end in a verifiable state, check each before the next, and order delivery so the sequence proves itself to a reviewer.\\\"\\ndisable-model-invocation: true\\n---\\n\\n# Sequence work into verifiable units\\n\\nOrder work as a sequence of small units, each ending in a state you can check, and don't advance until the current one is green.\\n\\n**Why:** A break caught at the unit that caused it is cheap to localize. A break caught after a batch is buried, and you have already built further on a broken base. Sequencing those same units into a delivery a reviewer can replay turns \\\"trust me\\\" into \\\"watch it go red, then green.\\\"\\n\\n**Execution.** In a sweep, migration, or any run of similar edits, verify each change before starting the next. Each unit is a before/after bracket: known-good state, one change, run the check, then proceed. Rebase onto clean trunk first so every check measures against the real baseline. When a lever does the edits, the per-unit check is nearly free. Run it anyway.\\n\\n**Delivery.** Stack commits and PRs in the order that proves the work. The canonical shape is the failing test first, then the fix on top. Other story orders are a subtraction before the reshape, a baseline capture before the treatment, the scaffold before the feature.
